chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
title: Critic bias in reviews, Paul Whiteman and Benny Goodman
summary: Ridley notes critics qualify praise of black artists, and they trace it from James Reese Europe and Whiteman to Goodman.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That's the interesting thing out there, sort of like a survey over the past 15 years of going back and looking at all the reviews by a certain critic with major newspapers and it's very interesting to notice that whenever he does a review on black artists, he goes to state oh there's traces of this person and traces of that person. He can't ever say nothing straight ahead about the individual. But when he talks about

about a shite artist, I meanall the superlatives just start flowing home, magnificent, oh the greatest this, oh blah blah blah, horp de doo, you know. And I know I'm not being paranoid because it's very black and white. I see and just comparing. I mean how on the one hand are you going to talk about a person who is a great musician and just say that it's just a so so performance and then you talk about this person over here and you're ranting and raving. I mean it's got to be a part of the whole mentality that's very racist in orientation.

And that's what I mean by conspiracy in that it's just that general innate kind of subliminal thing that those white critics and even the booking agents and everything that really have about people like what you just said. All these people come to see this little black trumpet player.

And the parallel like you say has happened all throughout history. Look at James Rees Europe who was around in the early 19 teens and the twenties, early twenties and they had to talk about Paul Whiteman who was the king of jazz. But James Reese Europe was the one that really was doing it. He was the one that had the 369th band that was playing jazz and went over there to Europe and just drove them crazy over there. And Eubie Blake and all of them, Noble Sissle and all of them talked about it, you know.
And then you get the Swing period and they will talk about Benny Goodman.
You know we had Paul Whiteman and now we've got Benny Goodman and then Fletcher Henderson, Sy Oliver.
Jimmy Mundy. You know they used to write all the music for them cats. And you've got Count Basie and all them different territory bands that was out there, hitting.
